seo.title: IELTS Reading Tips to Avoid Common Traps (2026)
seo.description: Practical IELTS reading tips for 2026: beat True/False/Not Given, matching headings, synonym traps and word limits, with a timing plan that works.

content:
Getting a high score in IELTS Reading is not about reading faster. It is about knowing how the questions are designed to mislead you, and having a method for each type. Many students from Kochi and across Kerala understand the passages well but still lose marks to the same traps: matching words instead of meaning, confusing False with Not Given, and running out of time on the last passage. These IELTS reading tips for 2026 cover the most common traps and exactly how to avoid them.

Know the test before you plan your strategy

The IELTS Academic Reading test has 40 questions on three sections, with a total text length of roughly 2,150 to 2,750 words. You have 60 minutes, and this includes the time to transfer your answers, so on paper there is no extra time at the end. On the computer-delivered test you type answers directly as you go. Each correct answer earns one mark, and your total is converted to a band score from 1 to 9.

General Training Reading also has 40 questions in 60 minutes, but the texts are taken from everyday and workplace sources such as notices, advertisements and handbooks. The traps described below apply to both versions.

IELTS reading tips for the most common traps

Trap 1: Matching keywords instead of meaning

IELTS almost always paraphrases. The words in the question are rarely the exact words in the passage, and when you do see an identical word, it is often a distractor placed near the wrong answer. Focus on the idea, not the word.

Question says Passage might say
increased sharply rose dramatically, soared, climbed steeply
children young people, minors, under-12s
not expensive affordable, reasonably priced, low-cost
researchers believe according to scientists, it is widely thought
at the beginning initially, in its early stages, originally

Building this awareness takes practice. Our older post on the significance of keywords and synonyms in IELTS Reading has more examples.

Trap 2: Confusing False and Not Given

This is the trap that costs the most marks. The official definitions are clear:

  • True: the statement agrees with the information in the text.
  • False: the statement contradicts the information in the text.
  • Not Given: the statement neither agrees with nor contradicts the text.

Yes/No/Not Given questions work in the same way, but they test the writer’s views or claims rather than facts.

Worked example. Passage: “The bridge was completed in 1932, two years later than originally planned, and was at the time the longest of its kind in the region.”

  • The bridge was finished behind schedule. True (two years later than planned).
  • The bridge was completed in 1930. False (the text says 1932, a direct contradiction).
  • The bridge cost more than expected. Not Given (cost is never mentioned, even though delays often increase costs).

That last one is the classic trap: your own logic or general knowledge suggests an answer, but the passage does not say it. The official guidance specifically warns against using what you already know about the topic. If you cannot point to the words that prove or contradict the statement, it is Not Given.

Trap 3: Matching headings that echo a detail

In matching headings questions, there are always more headings than paragraphs, and wrong headings often describe a detail or example from the paragraph rather than its main idea.

  1. Read the paragraph first, not the headings. Focus on the first two sentences and the last sentence.
  2. Summarise the main idea in five or six words of your own.
  3. Now find the heading that matches your summary.
  4. Be suspicious of a heading that repeats a striking word from the middle of the paragraph.

Some candidates find it helps to do matching headings after the other questions on the same passage, because by then you understand the text better.

Trap 4: Ignoring word limits

For sentence, summary, note, table and diagram completion and short-answer questions, the instructions set a limit such as “NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER”. If you write more than the limit, you lose the mark, even if the meaning is right. Hyphenated words such as “check-in” count as one word. Also copy spellings exactly from the passage, because incorrect spelling is marked wrong.

Trap 5: Missing negative and limiting words

Words such as NOT, EXCEPT, only, all, never, always, most and some can completely change the answer. “Most experts agree” is not the same as “all experts agree”. When a statement contains a strong word like “always” or “only”, check that the passage is equally strong.

Trap 6: Losing track of question order

For several question types, including multiple choice, sentence completion, matching sentence endings and short-answer questions, the answers appear in the same order as the information in the text. Use this to your advantage: if you have found answers 3 and 5, answer 4 is somewhere between them. Summary, note, table and diagram completion answers may not follow this order, and matching questions can come from anywhere in the passage.

Skimming and scanning: when to use each

  • Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea. Spend about two minutes skimming each passage before the questions: title, first lines of paragraphs and any diagram.
  • Scanning means searching for a specific detail such as a name, date or number. Use it for matching information and completion questions.

Once you have scanned to the right place, slow down and read those sentences carefully. Most mistakes happen when students scan well but then read the key sentence too quickly. For more techniques, see our quick tricks for the IELTS Reading test.

Time management in 2026

With 40 questions in 60 minutes, you have an average of about 90 seconds per question, but the passages usually get harder as you go. A practical plan:

  • Section 1: about 17 minutes
  • Section 2: about 20 minutes
  • Section 3: about 23 minutes

If one question is taking too long, make a sensible guess, mark it and move on. There is no negative marking, so never leave a blank. On paper, remember that transfer time is included in the 60 minutes: either write answers on the answer sheet as you go, or stop with enough time to transfer them carefully. On the computer, you can flag questions and use the on-screen timer to keep pace.

Eliminate wrong options logically

In multiple choice questions, cross out options that are clearly wrong first. Typical wrong options are true according to the passage but do not answer the question, use the same words as the text but change the meaning, or go further than the text (for example, “always” when the text says “often”). When you are down to two options, return to the passage and find the exact sentence that decides between them.

How to practise effectively

  • Use official or Cambridge practice tests, which reflect the real question style.
  • After each test, review every wrong answer and write down which trap caught you.
  • Practise under timed conditions at least once a week.
  • Read widely in English: quality newspapers, popular science magazines and longer articles.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between False and Not Given in IELTS Reading?

False means the passage contradicts the statement. Not Given means the passage does not say whether the statement is true or false. If you cannot find words in the text that prove or disprove the statement, choose Not Given.

Is there extra time to transfer answers in IELTS Reading?

No. The 60 minutes includes transfer time, so on the paper test you must transfer your answers within the hour. On the computer-delivered test you type your answers directly.

Should I read the whole passage before the questions?

A quick skim of about two minutes is usually enough to understand the structure. Then read the questions and go back to the relevant parts in detail. Reading every word slowly first often leaves too little time for Section 3.
